newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Bishops say rights infringed in Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: Bishops say rights infringed in Kabila's Congo.

text.p: Roman Catholic bishops in the Democratic Republic of the Congo say that human rights have been infringed since President Laurent Kabila's forces toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May.
The bishops, outspoken critics of human rights abuses and lack of democracy under Mobutu in the former Zaire, expressed concern about the future.
"Some new authorities carry out acts which do not respect human dignity," they said in a statement sent to Reuters, adding that the local population was worried.
"The change of people at the helm of the country is not enough. The demise of the former regime does not automatically bring about the desired change," they added.
The statement, signed on June 28 by 11 bishops and Cardinal Frederic Etsou, express particular concern at cases of score-settling and revenge killings.

Kinshasa residents say that since Kabila's Rwandan-backed forces arrived people have increasingly taken the law into their own hands. Thieves and house-breakers caught red-handed have been lynched or burned to death.
The Kinshasa interim governor has promised to punish anyone resorting to private justice but nothing has been done to date.
Kabila's forces toppled Mobutu after a seven-month war. He declared himself president with sweeping powers and banned political activity.

The U.N. is trying to negotiate terms with Kabila's administration for a U.N. probe into a separate rights issue -- allegations that his forces or their allies massacred Rwandan Hutus during their march across the then Zaire.
The bishops' statement also urged steps to prevent any return to war and called for a unified army. "To set up a unified army, private militias must be banned," it said.
